'''Helen Louise Caines''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FInstP}} is the Horace D. Taft Professor of Physics at [[Yale University]] and a member of the [[Yale Wright Laboratory]].<ref name="taft">{{cite web|url=https://news.yale.edu/2024/03/06/helen-caines-appointed-horace-d-taft-professor-physics|title=Helen Caines appointed Horace D. Taft Professor of Physics|website=YaleNews|date=2024-03-06|access-date=2025-02-22}}</ref> She is a [[nuclear physics|nuclear physicist]] who studies the [[quark–gluon plasma]] (QGP) using [[heavy-ion collision]]s. She was the elected co-spokesperson of the [[STAR experiment]] at the [[Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider]] (RHIC) from 2017 to 2023 and is also a collaborator on the [[ALICE experiment]] at the [[Large Hadron Collider]] and the ePIC experiment at the future [[Electron-Ion Collider]].<ref name="taft" />

== Education ==
Caines studied physics at the [[University of Birmingham]], graduating in 1992.<ref name=star>{{cite web|url=http://star.physics.yale.edu/~caines/CV/cv.html|title=Helen Caines|website=star.physics.yale.edu|access-date=2018-12-13}}</ref> She earned her PhD at Birmingham in 1996, with doctoral research conducted on the [[NA49 experiment]] at the [[Super Proton Synchrotron|CERN SPS]], where she studied [[strangeness]] production in lead–lead collisions as a probe of [[quark–gluon plasma]] formation.<ref name=helphd>{{cite thesis|first=Helen Louise|last=Caines|year=1996|publisher=University of Birmingham|title=A study of strangeness production in Pb-Pb collisions at 158GeV nucleon|degree=PhD|id={{copac|911151465}}|url=https://birmingham-primo.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=44BIR_ALMA_DS21110718810004871&context=L&vid=44BIR_VU1&search_scope=CSCOP_44BIR_DEEP&tab=local&lang=en_US|oclc=911151465}}</ref>

== Career ==
[[File:STAR Detector at Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider.jpg|thumb|The STAR Detector at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider]]
After completing her doctorate, Caines joined [[Ohio State University]] as a postdoctoral researcher in 1996, working on the [[STAR experiment]] at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=https://news.yale.edu/2017/07/12/yale-s-helen-caines-takes-leadership-role-international-star-experiment|title=Yale's Helen Caines takes a leadership role in international experiment|last=Shelton|first=Jim|date=2017-07-12|website=YaleNews|language=en|access-date=2018-12-13}}</ref> She was elected a junior representative of the STAR collaboration in 1998.<ref name=":0" />

Caines was appointed assistant professor of physics at [[Yale University]] in 2004 and promoted to associate professor in 2010.<ref name=":0" /> Along with Zhangbu Xu, she served as elected co-spokesperson of the STAR experiment from 2017 to 2023, overseeing a collaboration of more than 60 institutions in 13 countries.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="taft" /> In 2024, she was appointed the Horace D. Taft Professor of Physics.<ref name="taft" /> She serves as Director of Graduate Studies for the Yale Department of Physics.

In addition to STAR, Caines is a collaborator on the [[ALICE experiment]] at the [[Large Hadron Collider]] at [[CERN]] and has joined the ePIC collaboration, the experiment selected for the future [[Electron-Ion Collider]].<ref name="taft" /> She served on the [[Nuclear Science Advisory Committee]] (NSAC) of the [[United States Department of Energy]] and contributed to the United States Long Range Plan for Nuclear Physics.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Akiba|first1=Yasuyuki|last2=Angerami|first2=Aaron|last3=Caines|first3=Helen|last4=Frawley|first4=Anthony|last5=Heinz|first5=Ulrich|last6=Jacak|first6=Barbara|last7=Jia|first7=Jiangyong|last8=Lappi|first8=Tuomas|last9=Li|first9=Wei|date=2015|title=The Hot QCD White Paper: Exploring the Phases of QCD at RHIC and the LHC|arxiv=1502.02730|bibcode=2015arXiv150202730A}}</ref>

== Research ==
[[File:View of gold ions collision.jpg|thumb|The collision of two gold ions at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]].]]
Caines' research focuses on understanding the behaviour of nuclear matter under extreme conditions of temperature and density, using heavy-ion collisions to create and study the [[quark–gluon plasma]] (QGP), the state of matter believed to have existed microseconds after the [[Big Bang]].

Her early work at RHIC contributed to establishing the properties of the QGP through measurements of hadronic particle production in the [[STAR detector]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Caines|first=Helen|date=2003|title=STAR results from the first year at RHIC|journal=Pramana|language=en|volume=60|issue=4|pages=627–638|doi=10.1007/BF02705163|issn=0973-7111|bibcode=2003Prama..60..627C|s2cid=120358633}}</ref> She has played a central role in the RHIC beam energy scan programme, studying Au+Au collisions at centre-of-mass energies from {{math|{{sqrt|''s''{{sub|NN}}}}}} = 7.7 to 200 GeV to map the [[QCD phase diagram]] and search for the predicted critical point of the transition between hadronic matter and the QGP.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Caines|first=Helen|date=2014|title=A Snapshot of our Experimental Knowledge Circa Winter 2012-13|journal=Journal of Physics: Conference Series|language=en|volume=509|issue=1|article-number=012001|doi=10.1088/1742-6596/509/1/012001|issn=1742-6596|bibcode=2014JPhCS.509a2001C|doi-access=free}}</ref>

A widely noted result from Caines' group was the measurement of global [[hyperon]] [[Polarization (waves)|polarization]] in heavy-ion collisions, which demonstrated that the QGP is the most [[vorticity|vortical]] fluid ever observed.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.yalescientific.org/2018/01/whats-hot-dense-and-spins-like-crazy/|title=What's Hot, Dense, and Spins Like Crazy?|last=Sanchez-Maes|first=Sophia|date=2018-01-17|website=yalescientific.org|publisher=Yale Scientific Magazine|language=en-US|access-date=2018-12-13}}</ref> She has also been involved in the isobar collision programme, comparing [[ruthenium]]–ruthenium and [[zirconium]]–zirconium collisions to test for the [[chiral magnetic effect]] in QCD matter.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://phys.org/news/2018-03-relativistic-heavy-ion-collider-18th.html|title=Relativistic heavy ion collider begins 18th year of experiments|website=phys.org|language=en-us|access-date=2018-12-13}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bnl.gov/newsroom/news.php?a=112738|title=Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider Begins 18th Year of Experiments|website=bnl.gov|publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory|access-date=2018-12-13}}</ref>

More recently, Caines has applied [[machine learning]] techniques to heavy-ion physics, including the use of [[artificial neural network]]s to identify quark and gluon jets in the dense environment of heavy-ion collisions.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=APS -2017 Fall Meeting of the APS Division of Nuclear Physics - Event - Identifying Jets Using {{sic|Artif|ical|nolink=y}} Neural Networks|url=http://meetings.aps.org/Meeting/DNP17/Session/EA.77|journal=Bulletin of the American Physical Society|publisher=American Physical Society|volume=62|issue=11}}</ref>

== Teaching and service ==
Caines developed the course ''Being Human in STEM'' at Yale, which examines how socioeconomic background, gender, race, religion, and sexuality shape the experience of working in [[STEM fields|STEM]]. The course was modelled on a similar programme at [[Amherst College]].<ref name=":2">{{cite web|url=https://yaledailynews.com/blog/2016/12/09/class-examines-inclusivity-in-stem/|title=Class examines inclusivity in STEM|first=Ellen|last=Kan|date=December 9, 2016|website=yaledailynews.com|language=en|access-date=2018-12-13}}</ref>

She has served on the [[American Physical Society]]'s Committee on the Status of Women in Physics and the Committee on Minorities in Physics.<ref name="taft" /> She has organized major conferences in her field, including the Critical Point and Onset of Deconfinement (CPOD) International Conference and the Strangeness in Quark Matter International Conference.<ref name="taft" />

== Awards and honours ==
* 2003 – [[Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council]] Advanced Research Fellowship<ref name=star/>
* 2005 – ''Enseignant Invité'' fellowship, [[University of Strasbourg]]
* 2008 – Elected [[Fellow of the Institute of Physics]] (FInstP)<ref name=":0" />
* 2012 – APS Woman Physicist of the Month
* 2019 – Elected Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://physics.yale.edu/news/helen-caines-associate-professor-physics-elected-fellow-american-physical-society|title=Helen Caines (Associate Professor of Physics) elected a Fellow of the American Physical Society|website=physics.yale.edu|access-date=2018-12-13}}</ref>
* 2024 – Appointed Horace D. Taft Professor of Physics<ref name="taft" />
